notes: Every answer stayed within its section's word limit. Counted with headings, the longest used about 275 of 300 words. Length never separated answers; what separated them was whether each one answered the requirement asked.

About one answer in seven answered a different requirement. Examples are site setup and path mapping under B.3, B.4, B.6 and B.7, a generic site build under B.5, Concierge reporting under C.5 and D.6, and Coworker features under F.1. These scored 1 or 2 however polished they were.

Brochure answers gave the panel nothing it could hold a vendor to. They carried Adobe capability statements, the client's name dropped into 'For Cedar Prairie Mutual Insurance Company, we will...', and long prerequisite lists, and committed to no deliverables, timeline or effort. Nine answers open with 'You told us:' and restate the RFP before answering.

Several estimates were hard to trust. The same text recurred with different hours for the same scope: B.8 A and D at 80 and 160 hours, F.4 A and D at 48 and 112 hours a month, B.2 A and B at 240 and 320. Effort was often pushed to another answer ('adds no hours of its own', 'hours not repeated here') or given as a wide range (60 to 240 hours). No answer tied its work to the RFP's ten-month launch or twelve-month CJA dates; timelines were relative ('during the build').

The strongest answers used Cedar Prairie's own facts: Drupal 9, 3,400 pages and 900 PDFs with rate filings, Akamai, Compliance approval, Genesys Cloud, Salesforce FSC, Power BI and the 35 marketers. They named concrete deliverables, gave itemized hours and disclosed separately licensed add-ons (Workfront, Marketo Qualifier). Weaker answers lost credibility: Dispatcher validation and Core Components on an Edge Delivery build, SharePoint or Google Drive authoring and 'Adobe's managed CDN or your own' when the RFP had already fixed AEM and Akamai, and an unfilled placeholder in F.3.

notes: About one answer in five did not answer the requirement asked and scored 1 or 2. The same AEM site-setup and path-mapping text was offered for accessibility (B.3 A), Core Web Vitals (B.4 D) and A/B testing (B.7 B), and text about Concierge reporting in CJA was offered for the Genesys handoff (C.5 A and D) and for consent (D.6 A).

Many answers were Adobe product description followed by a list of prerequisites, with no method, deliverables or effort (for example B.1 D, B.2 C, B.8 C, C.1 D, C.4 A, D.2 C, D.4 C, D.5 B). Accurate product statements alone did not earn more than a 5.

The best answer to each requirement was usually the one written from Cedar Prairie's own facts: Drupal 9 with 3,400 pages and 900 PDFs, rate filings, Akamai, Compliance approval, Genesys Cloud, Snowflake policy and claims data, Power BI, GLBA. Those answers had concrete steps, named deliverables, hours broken down and a specific risk. None reached 9 or 10, because even the best left gaps: core build hours never stated (B.1 A), thin search-engine steps (B.8 B), an unfilled support-hours placeholder (F.3 D).

Effort figures were often inconsistent or hard to believe. Identical text carried different hours (B.2: 240 against 320; B.8: 80 against 160; F.4: 48 against 112 a month). Some figures look too low for the work: 24 hours to roll out Coworker to 35 people, 240 hours to migrate 3,400 pages and 900 PDFs, 40 to 80 hours for a Genesys bridge. Others are unexplained, such as 256 hours to set up a Marketo instance the client already runs. Several answers moved their hours into another service ('adds no hours of its own', 'hours not repeated here').

Boilerplate sometimes contradicted the RFP or the chosen architecture: SharePoint or Google Drive authoring and 'Adobe's managed CDN or your own' when AEM Sites and Akamai are already decided; Core Components, editable templates and Dispatcher validation in an Edge Delivery build; an 'existing CMS' and purchase measures for an insurer; 'You told us' lines that restate the question instead of tailoring to it. Answers that named a product needing its own license (Workfront, Marketo Qualifier) or a real limit (only monitored prompts are measured, Concierge visitors are anonymous) read as more credible.

notes: Each requirement had exactly one answer built around our own situation (42,000 files, 430,000 contacts, five markets, Salesforce, Snowflake and Akamai, the 15 February and 2 August 2027 dates), and those seven scored 6 to 8; the other answers were generic and often described a neighbouring service (lead scoring for enquiry routing, template building for preference migration, site build or discovery for accessibility, AI-referred audiences for event design) instead of the requirement.

Commitments were the clearest divider: strong answers tied the work to our dates, split hours by component and named the staff time we must supply, while weak ones said only 'runs during the build' or gave no effort; even the strong answers name their proof (zero-overlap check, per-market consistency report, reconciliation tolerances) more than they describe it, point to hours held in other line items they do not state, and two leave unfilled placeholders ([NAMED ACCESSIBILITY REVIEWER], [SERVICE LEVEL SCHEDULE]) on points we asked them to name.

All 28 answers stayed within the 250-word limit, so length did not separate them; licensing was handled unevenly (CJA Select or higher is stated where the BI extension or audiences are used, but no answer explains whether publishing to Real-Time Customer Profile fits within the four products we are considering), and no answer addresses consent rules that differ across our five markets, which affect both email permissions in C.1 and analytics counts in D.1.

scores.why: A alone handles every part of the ask (file hashes and similar-name flags for duplicates, a proposed current revision for each manual family, required product and revision fields, engineer sign-off by product line with only signed rows loaded) and gives dates and split hours; B and C are the same generic Bulk Import and CSV migration and never mention duplicates, superseded manuals or engineers; D lists setup tasks plus an off-point Content Hub claim, with no outputs, timeline or effort.

Only D answers the question: a most-restrictive-wins rule for conflicts, unmatched suppressions still loaded, a suppression proof pack, a zero-overlap gate before the first send and its own 40 to 70 hours; A and B describe building program templates (A quotes the preference conflict and then ignores it), and C is generic instance setup that names 'Salesforce or Dynamics', so none of the three covers preferences, suppression or proof.

C is the only answer that designs the enquiry path (Salesforce keeps territory and assignment, email matching to existing leads or contacts, routing Smart Campaigns, a fallback list reviewed daily, split hours and the client's admin time), though repeated submissions and re-routing after a territory change are only implied; A, B and D offer a data audit, lead scoring and an MQL handoff, which is not what was asked.

B defines the download, the completed enquiry and the abandoned form precisely, keeps field values out of the schema, adds a payload scan on every release and per-market consistency tests with dates and hours, though it never says how events are collected (Web SDK, tags or a data layer) or what the counts are checked against; A, C and D answer a different requirement, AI-referred audiences published to Real-Time Customer Profile, which also cuts across the client's rule of no new customer data platform.

C goes at the actual dispute: a signed metric dictionary, metrics defined once as data view components, a reconciliation page with published tolerances, a plain statement that no CJA data is copied into Snowflake, and the CJA Select entitlement; A, B and D only connect a generic BI tool through the BI extension and check it against Workspace without ever reconciling to Salesforce sales totals, B adds dashboard briefs and measure guides, and D gives no effort or timeline.

A covers templates in three languages, forms and a sized sample of PDF manuals, separates build-gating automated scans from manual keyboard and screen-reader tests and ends in a signed acceptance statement, but names its verifier only as a placeholder and claims template testing adds no hours; D's method for templates is sound, but it skips published documents and the verifier and spans 60 to 240 hours; B is discovery boilerplate, and C is a 400-hour site build that never mentions accessibility.

D alone covers incident ownership (third-party faults go to the client's IT owners), checks on the Salesforce sync and the specification feed, release checks, reporting, monthly hours per product and a stated boundary for separately estimated work, though its monitoring is a periodic review and its service levels are an unfilled placeholder; A lists monthly tasks for the four products with no incidents, hours or boundary, and B and C each cover only one product.

notes: In every requirement exactly one answer was written for Vennor Quay (A for B.1 and E.1, B for D.1, C for C.2 and D.3, D for C.1 and E.5). The other three were reusable service descriptions, often for a different requirement: program templates for C.1, lead scoring for C.2, AI-referred audiences for D.1, a site build for E.1.

Boilerplate repeats word for word across answers: the CJA sentence about call-centre and point-of-sale data (for a firm that sells only through dealers, and with no word on its Genesys Cloud contact centre), the Bulk Import list of cloud storage sources, 'Salesforce or Dynamics' and 'Power BI, Tableau or Looker'. To a panel this reads as text that was not written for this RFP.

'You told us:' lines restate the RFP, and sometimes the question itself, and then the rest of the answer ignores what was quoted (B.1 B, C.1 A, C.2 D, D.3 B, E.1 D, E.5 C). That reads worse than not quoting it at all.

The tailored answers are concrete and mostly accurate, with credible split effort, the client's staff time named and optional work separated. notes: Each requirement had one answer clearly written for Vennor Quay that used our numbers, dates, systems and constraints and answered each sub-question. The other three were mostly generic product text. That gap decided every requirement, not length: all 28 answers were within the word limit.

Several weaker answers open with 'You told us:' and repeat text from our RFP, in two cases the question itself (B.1 B, E.1 D), and then never deal with it (also C.1 A, C.2 D, D.3 B, E.5 C). Repeating our problem without solving it reads like a template and costs credibility.

Off-topic answers came up again and again: AI-referred audiences for event collection (three of the four D.1 answers), lead scoring and an MQL handoff for enquiry routing, program templates for the preference migration, and a site build for accessibility. notes: Each requirement had one answer written around Vennor Quay's own facts (430,000 contacts, 42,000 files, three languages across five markets, the 15 February and 2 August 2027 dates, the systems it is keeping) that worked through every sub-question. The other three were mostly accurate descriptions of a related standard service (program templates for C.1, lead scoring for C.2, a site build for E.1, AI-referred audiences for D.1), not answers to the question asked.

The one serious product-fit failure was in D.1, answers A, C and D. They rely on Experience Platform's Real-Time Customer Profile, which is used through Real-Time CDP or Journey Optimizer. Neither product is among the four this client is considering, and the client has ruled out a customer data platform. None of the three says it depends on them.

Boilerplate cost credibility. Several answers open with 'You told us:' and a line quoted from the RFP (in B.1 B, the question itself) that the answer then never takes up. Others hedge with 'Where your CRM is Salesforce', 'Salesforce or Dynamics', 'Power BI, Tableau or Looker' or 'your own BI tool' even though the client has named its systems.

Even the strongest answers had fixable defects. Two leave placeholders unfilled: '[NAMED ACCESSIBILITY REVIEWER]' in E.1 A and '[SERVICE LEVEL SCHEDULE]' in E.5 D. They also say little about Adobe's side of the work. E.5 D checks the automatic AEM version updates 'before your sign-off', but Adobe applies those updates to AEM as a Cloud Service without any client sign-off. D.1 B never says how events are collected from the pages.

Outside D.1, the Adobe statements were broadly accurate in every answer: Bulk Import from cloud storage with CSV metadata, metadata forms, the two-way Salesforce sync for leads, contacts and campaigns, and BI extension access through data views. So the scores turned on fit and on whether the question was answered. The better answers also tied effort to dates, named the client staff time needed, and separated included work from optional or separately estimated work, as the RFP asks.
